1.1: 1.1 Preface. In Hebrew SOPHETIMATHANAS, in the Synopsis. This book is called Judges, because after the death of Joshua son of Nun, God saved his people, pressed by the nations of the Canaanites that had been left, through judges; the deeds and the time of life of each of whom are contained in this volume, etc. They were thirteen in number: and their years were four hundred and eleven. Isidore, in the book of Judges, ch. 1: The history of the book of Judges indicates no small sacraments of mysteries. For after Joshua the Judges succeed, as after Christ the apostles and the rulers of the churches, to govern the faithful, whom he himself leads to the hope of the eternal promise. Throughout this volume are contained the faults of the Jewish people, and their servitude and their cry and the compassion of God. For many years they served on account of their sins, and being converted were set free: because our sins give strength to enemies; and when we do evil in the sight of the Lord, our adversaries, that is, the demons, are strengthened. But when we are converted, God raises up judges and saviors, that is, leaders and teachers whom he sends to the help of those who cry to God with their whole heart. Augustine, question 1 on the book of Judges: At the end of the book of Joshua son of Nun the narrator briefly carried the history forward to the point at which the children of Israel turned aside to worship strange gods. But in this book he returns to the order, how the consequences came about after the death of Joshua son of Nun. The book does not therefore begin from that time at which the people lapsed into worshiping idols: but from earlier times, the intervening periods being inserted, in which those things were done, after it comes to them.
1.2: 1.2 And the Lord said: Judah shall go up, etc. The same, question 2. It is asked whether some man was called Judah, or whether he called the tribe itself so, as was customary, etc., up to: then the tribe of Simeon also was taken up to fight.
1.12: 1.12 And he said, etc. Augustine, question 3. Whoever shall strike the city of letters and take it, I will give him my daughter to wife. This is recorded in the book of Joshua, etc., up to: nor yet do I think it is in vain that Scripture has twice recorded this of the daughter of Caleb given as the prize of the victor.
1.19: 1.19 Nor could he. The same, question 5 on Judges. In this very thing was the Lord, etc., up to: while the Apostle says: Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, etc. (2 Cor. 12).
1.21: 1.21 The Jebusite. Augustine, question 7 on Judges. Above the same city is read, etc., up to: not without him did they hold the land they possessed.
1.27: 1.27 Manasseh. Augustine, question 8. And Manasseh did not inherit Beth-shean, etc., up to: that the Scythians once held almost all of Asia.
1.34: 1.34 And he confined. Augustine, question 11 on Judges. And the Amorites pressed hard the children of Dan in the mountain, for they did not permit them to come down, etc. This, however, is recorded in the book of Joshua son of Nun by anticipation; but here by recapitulation.
2.1: 2.1 And the angel went up. Augustine, question 12 on Judges. And the angel of the Lord went up, etc., up to: which he there recorded by anticipation.
2.3: 2.3 Therefore I was unwilling to destroy. Augustine, question 13 on Judges. From this we understand that some sins come from the wrath of God. For that the gods of the nations, among whom the Israelites wished to dwell, not having exterminated them, might be a stumbling block to them, that is, might make them stumble in their God, and live with him offended, God, indignant, threatened, which makes plain that it is a great sin. So Joshua dismissed. Augustine: This is repeated by recapitulation. For the death of Joshua son of Nun is also recorded in this book, so that as from the beginning all things may be briefly set forth, from when the Lord gave them the land, and how they lived under the judges, or what they suffered; and again, return is made to the order of the judges, from him who was first appointed.
2.7: 2.7 And they grew old. Adamantius, homily 1 on Judges. The elders who were with Joshua or after Joshua, etc., up to: but the days of the holy elders are long-lived and extended.
2.8: 2.8 He died. The same, homily 2. In Paul Jesus lives, etc., up to: and another generation arose, which knew not Jesus, etc. Adamantius, homily 2. And they served Baalim, etc., up to: we love with the whole soul and all our strength; we adore idols.
2.13: 2.13 Augustine, question 16 on the book of Judges. And they served Baal and Astaroth. Baal is said to be the name of Jupiter among those nations, etc., up to: he wished Juno to be mentioned in the plural. Augustine, question 17. But also in the psalm, etc., up to: they were not to be redeemed by a money price.
2.14: 2.14 And the Lord was angry. Origen, homily 2 on Judges. When anyone serves God, etc., up to: lest we be delivered to the devil.
3.5: 3.5 In the midst. Augustine, question 17 on Judges. In Exodus God says, etc., up to: their multitude would not allow the lands from which the adversaries were to be exterminated to be desert. And as to what he says: Lest wild beasts multiply against you; it would be strange if he did not wish bestial desires and lusts to be understood... for God could not exterminate men and not be able to exterminate beasts.
3.8: 3.8 Adamantius, homily 3. And the Lord delivered them, etc., up to: the most foul odor of pride gleams. Origen, homily 3 on Judges. See the kind Lord, etc., up to: who are designated through Othniel or Ehud.
3.10: 3.10 The Spirit of the Lord was upon him, etc. It is great praise of the first judge that the Spirit of the Lord came upon him: and by the Spirit of God he judged the people, which I do not remember being said of another to any great degree. There are today judges of the churches, to whom is given even the judgment of souls: but I do not know whether any is worthy to be filled with the Spirit of God. And he was in. Adamantius: After, namely, they cried to the Lord. Who among us sends forth so strong, so just a cry to the Lord, that the people may deserve to receive a judge whom the Spirit of God fills, that he might hold right judgment? Whence this book is called Judges, of those, namely, who judged the people of Israel, wonderful men, namely, as Joshua was. As is also the book of Kings, in which it is told how each of the kings reigned, and what he did, even evil: that the princes of the Church, namely, or judges, may imitate their good deeds and beware of the evil. And Israel served. Adamantius, as above. After eighteen years, etc., up to: to whom it will be said: Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I know you not: go into everlasting fire, etc. (Luke 13). The same: Divine Scripture also indicates the measures of punishment; above, eight years: here it says eighteen. It is certain that according to the measure of sin, and the delay of conversion, the times of chastisement are also bounded. For these eighteen years of servitude also passed, and it is not said that they cried to the Lord or were converted from their wickedness: but after.
3.15: 3.15 A savior. The same, homily 3. Saviors or judges, etc., up to: who says: I am the way, the truth, and the life (John 14). Who used both hands as the right. According to the spiritual understanding, all the saints are called ambidextrous, the devil and his princes, left-handed on both sides. For all that they do is left-handed and perverse, assigned to eternal fire with those who are on the left.
3.20: 3.20 Ehud went in, etc. Adamantius, homily 4. Ehud is interpreted praise. For using a cunning art and a praiseworthy deception, etc., up to: to whom it is said by the Lord: Well done, good servant, etc.
3.22: 3.22 Very fat. Augustine, question 21. It is rightly asked, etc., up to: so we find. Now Eglon was exceedingly fat.
3.25: 3.25 They took. The same, question 23. How did the servants of King Eglon open with a key what Ehud had not locked with a key? Or if he had locked it with a key, how did he not take it with him, so that they could not open it with a key? Therefore either another key was brought, or it was such a kind of lock that could be locked without a key and not opened without a key. For there are some such, like those which are called bolted.
3.31: 3.31 After him. Adamantius, homily 4. 70. Shamgar, that is, there a stranger. For all men of God are strangers in this world; as he who said: I am a stranger on the earth with you, and a sojourner, as all my fathers. This Shamgar, therefore, the Holy Spirit says is a stranger there, that is, here: for what is for the Holy Spirit, who is in heaven, there, is for us here. After him. Augustine, question 25. It is asked how after Ehud Shamgar fought for Israel and is said to have saved it. For it had not been taken captive or bound by the yoke of servitude. But he saved it thus, not because the enemy had harmed; but lest he be permitted to harm: who, it must be believed, had begun to make trial in war, and was repulsed by his victory. Who struck. Adamantius, homily 4. Shamgar struck the Philistines, six hundred men, etc., up to: that you may say confidently: But God forbid that I should glory, etc.
4.1: 4.1 And the children of Israel again. Origen, homily 4 on Judges. As though on account of the sins of the people the good leader died, etc., up to: and Jabin the prince of the Canaanites.
4.2: 4.2 Into the hands of Jabin king of Canaan. Adamantius, homily 4 on Judges. The commander of Jabin's army, etc., up to: either the people of the Church is governed, or the sense of each soul.
4.4: 4.4 There was. Adamantius, homily 5. According to the Apostle, etc., up to: because purity of mind confers this grace, not difference of sex. Deborah. Bee or speech, which signifies a prophetess; who composes the sweet honeycombs of heavenly doctrine and the sweet honeys of divine speech. Whence: How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth! (Psalm 118). And elsewhere: The judgments of the Lord, says the prophet, are more precious than gold and very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ibid. 10).
4.5: 4.5 And she sat under a palm tree, etc. Adamantius: See in what places prophecy sits, among the high places, namely, and the house of God. Nothing lowly, nothing base can be found around the seat of prophecy. As Solomon says: that she stands in the high places, namely the gates of cities, or dwells in the ramparts of the walls, or acts freely in high towers. Between the house of God, then, and the high places she is said to dwell. For she does not teach to seek the things that are on the earth, but those in heaven, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God. Thither she exhorts us to ascend: thither prophecy labors to move her disciples.
4.8: 4.8 If you come. Augustine, question 29 on Judges. What is it that Barak, answering Deborah, says, etc., up to: that is, he makes prosperous with me through an angel? Adamantius, homily 5. I will not go up unless you go up with me. You see how prophecy brought to those earlier ones the words of God, etc., up to: whose name is Jael, Sisera is handed over.
4.18: 4.18 Jael therefore went out. Adamantius, homily 5. Jael, a foreign woman, signifies the Church, etc., up to: delivered him to eternal sleep.
4.19: 4.19 Who opened. Adamantius, homily 5. Let every soul with this evangelical and apostolic milk lull and extinguish Sisera in itself, etc., up to: but one reward of victory will be given to the first and the last.
4.22: 4.22 And going out, etc. Adamantius, homily 5 on Judges. Jael meets him, etc., up to: by faithful touch he first obtains health.
5.1: 5.1 And Deborah and Barak sang, etc. Adamantius, homily 6 on Judges. If we remember what was said above, etc., up to: or the fault which came through our sloth. Hear, etc. The mountains melted before the face of the Lord. Adamantius: Receive with your ears, all you satraps. As satraps are lower than kings, etc., up to: worthily as a king you will be called to hear the divine words.
5.6: 5.6 In. The paths are said to have been still, which in the days of Shamgar leader of Israel were occupied by the enemies and they did not dare to go up to the house of the Lord to pray; from whom Shamgar is not written to have fully delivered them.
5.9: 5.9 My heart loves. Adamantius, homily 6. My heart toward those things which are prepared for this Israel. As if my heart, my mind, my sense, and my whole mind tends to that, looks to that which is arranged and prepared for Israel. Whence: I count all things that are in the world as dung, that I may gain Christ, etc. (Phil. 3).
5.10: 5.10 You who of your own will. Of whom it is said, You who willingly offered your souls to danger, etc., because they submitted themselves to the law of God and his service, meditating day and night on his law. You who ride upon shining asses. Adamantius: Mighty peoples, bless the Lord, because you ride upon beasts, etc. Our body is a beast of burden: for it is given for the aid and service of the soul. To the inner man it is said: He who rides upon the beast, that is, his body, and has become superior to bodily desires, and moderates the movements of the body with the rein of reason, that he may bless the Lord.
5.11: 5.11 They were crushed. As if to say, although God is to be praised always and everywhere, is not he rather to be praised and blessed here, who overthrew our enemies, as he overthrew the Egyptians in the Red Sea? There let them be told. Adamantius, Seventy: The just were strengthened in Israel. Among other nations, those who are stronger in bodily strength are called mighty in battle: but in Israel, those who are more just; because justice, though weak in strength, conquers. But injustice, though it has many strong warriors, is overcome. Therefore in our nation either we overcome through justice, or are conquered through injustice.
5.12: 5.12 Arise, arise. In the Hebrew it is not so: but awake with the spirit, namely of prophecy, for the perfect teachers provoke Deborah to awake with the spirit of prophecy and of praise.
5.15: 5.15 Divided. The voice of Deborah rebuking Reuben, who did not obey the command of the Lord with his brothers to defeat the enemies, but, terrified and unbelieving of the words of the Lord, divided himself from them; and therefore the high-minded was found proud. Whence in the spirit of prophecy he is rebuked thus: Why do you dwell between two borders? etc. In the Hebrew, however, two is not found.
5.21: 5.21 He dragged their corpses, etc. Into the Red Sea, which is Kadumim, interpreted of the ancients: because ancient miracles were done there when the children of Israel passed through and the Egyptians perished: so that for the corpses of the Egyptians the fish and beasts of the Red Sea have the corpses of the Canaanites. Adamantius, homily 7 on Judges. They are not said to have prevailed over the people of God while they keep the precepts, etc., up to: when we are forsaken by the grace of God.
6.3: 6.3 And when he had sown. The same, homily 7. Israel suffered these things, etc., up to: glorified by his death, washed in blood.
6.8: 6.8 Who sent a prophet to them, who spoke: Thus says, etc. Augustine, question 31 on Judges. Why the name of this prophet is not given, etc., up to: why may not an angel be called a prophet? Isidore, on Judges, vol. 5. Gideon signifies Christ: who, under the shadow of the holy cross, established in the predestined mystery of the future incarnation, with the rectitude of judgment, like a rod, separated the election of the saints from the chaff of vices.
6.17: 6.17 Give me a sign. Adamantius, homily 8. A learned man, having the example of his predecessor Joshua, acts more cautiously. For he knew that the angels of darkness can transform themselves into angels of light: therefore he examines the spirit, whether it be of God. For the spiritual man examines all things. So his predecessor Joshua son of Nun, when he had seen the prince of the heavenly host, asks: Are you ours, or of our adversaries? So Gideon tests the angelic vision by the diversity and change of the signs.
6.18: 6.18 Bringing. Augustine, question 35 on Judges. It must be noted, etc., up to: as though to be helped by the presence of his holiness.
6.19: 6.19 He went in. Gregory, Morals, book 3, ch. 17. Gideon, when he was threshing the grain from the chaff, etc., up to: but also wipe away whatever in himself is shamefully bound by thoughts. Isidore: The bull which the father had assigned to deceits, Gideon killed, and another of seven years he sacrificed to God; in which he shows that after the coming of Christ all the sacrifices of the Gentiles are to be abolished, and only the sacrifice of the passion of Christ is now to be offered to God for the redemption of the people. For he himself is the seven-year-old calf, full, namely, of the sevenfold Spirit.
6.33: 6.33 Then. Adamantius: The Midianites gathered against Israel, etc., up to: they attack the people of God, namely with pagans and Jews. In the valley of Jezreel. The same: Which is interpreted the seed of God. For the adversaries do not dare to go there, etc., up to: because he is set on the summit of spiritual understanding.
6.36: 6.36 If you save. Adamantius, homily 8 on Judges. Since there are many and innumerable signs, etc., up to: on which no moisture of the divine word poured.
6.37: 6.37 On the threshing floor. Origen, homily 8. Not anywhere, not in a field, nor in a woodland, but on the threshing floor where the harvest is, etc., up to: let us with a clean heart recline at the banquet of the bridegroom Jesus Christ. If the dew be on the fleece only, etc. Augustine: In the testing of Gideon, what the Lord wished to foretell he shows: in the fleece wet and the whole floor dry all around, he figures the first people of Israel, where were the saints with heavenly grace as with spiritual rain; and afterward, the floor wet, the fleece dried, he figures the Church of God spread through the whole world, having heavenly grace not in a fleece as in a veil, but in the open, the former people as though estranged and dried from the dew of that same grace.
6.39: 6.39 I pray, etc. Adamantius, homily 8. In the account of the second sign also, etc., up to: the grace of the divine dew is poured on the whole earth.
7.3: 7.3 Whoever is fearful, etc. Adamantius, homily 9. Jesus cries the same today, etc., up to: so among enormous and unspeakable crimes the crime of fear and dread is placed. Seventy: The fearful is he who, as with a young vice, before he sees evils, is terrified by thought alone, a cold dread coursing through his limbs, so that he is undone not so much by the sight of evils as by the hearing and expectation. Therefore, according to the Seventy, he is called fearful of heart, for this vice remains fixed in the heart and in the inmost parts of the mind. The timid, however, is he who at first sight trembles at the encounter, yet is not terrified with his whole heart, but can be restored and encouraged again.
7.4: 7.4 The people are still. Adamantius, homily 9. As I see, those who were first rejected, etc., up to: nor is he laid prone by the thirst of sin.
7.5: 7.5 Those who with hand and tongue. Adamantius, homily 9. He says they lap the water with hand and tongue, etc., up to: and they bear the perfect number of the Trinity.
7.6: 7.6 The number of them was, etc. Augustine, question 47 on Judges. And the number of those who lapped with their hand, with their tongue, was three hundred men. Most Latin codices do not have with their hand, but only with their tongue, etc., up to: David also calls himself, as contemptible, a dog.
7.13: 7.13 He struck it and overthrew it. Gregory, Morals, book 30, ch. 25. Of this war through the prophet, etc., up to: that the sword of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.
7.16: 7.16 And he divided. The same, ibid. They were led to the river, etc., up to: in the left a trumpet, in the right he holds a pitcher.
7.20: 7.20 And when they had broken the pitchers. Adamantius, homily 9. They carry pitchers, etc., up to: that we may deserve to obtain victory from him.
8.27: 8.27 And Gideon made of it an ephod, etc. Augustine, question 41 on Judges. It is asked what the Ephod or Ephot is, etc., up to: that so the numerous offspring of sons perished, as Scripture afterwards testifies. Augustine: It must be understood that it is said by prolepsis that Gideon made the Ephod against the law of God from the gold taken from the defeated enemies, so that it might be said at once whence the gold was and what was done with it. For this sin was committed at the end of Gideon's days: when the evils followed which Scripture appends, after it said for how many years the land was quiet in the days of Gideon. After. The same, question 43. And it came to pass, when Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned away and fornicated after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their covenant that he should be their god, etc. Both Baalim and Baal-berith are to be understood as idols. The transgression and fornication of the people after the death of Gideon is therefore greater than during his life on account of the Ephod. Which, even if it was done unlawfully, was nevertheless of the sacraments of the tabernacle: but this idolatry has no false defense of paternal religion. Whence, even if the Ephod of Gideon was not made at the end of his time, but earlier, God so patiently bore it that peace persisted in the land, because although what he had forbidden was done, yet there was not a distant departure from him who had commanded something like this to be made in his tabernacle in his honor. But now graver things were committed, and he would not have the open fornication of the people after idols go unpunished.
9.5: 9.5 And Jotham remained. Isidore: The younger son, who escaped the sword of the enemy by fleeing, signifies the remnant of Israel who will believe in the last time, and will escape the sword of Antichrist; he went up to the summit of Mount Gerizim: because no one can either prophesy or escape the persecution of Antichrist unless he has first ascended the mountain of blessing, that is, to the height of faith and virtues: for this is Mount Gerizim, which is assigned by Moses for blessing. Isidore, on Judges, vol. 5. If this deed were not mystical, etc., up to: he will bring on persecution that he may kill all the saints.
9.10: 9.10 And they said. The same, ibid. The trees of the forest are fruitless men, etc., up to: and brought the sweetest fatness of Christ with glory and honor. The same, ibid. The vine is Christ, who said: I am the true vine (John 15). Because therefore the people who serve Antichrist are given over to a reprobate mind to believe a lie, that is, Antichrist, since they would not believe the truth, that is, Christ, they are rejected from the kingdom of the vine, that is, of Christ; and from the olive, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and from the fig, that is, the sweetness of the divine law. And they said. The same: The bramble is a kind of thorn bush, which the common people call the bear-briar, exceedingly rough and thorny, by which Antichrist is signified, about to lay waste the human race with all harshness and ferocity: and fire shall come out of the bramble, that is, iniquity from Antichrist, and will devour all who trust in him together with him.
9.23: 9.23 And he sent. Augustine, question 45 on Judges. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem. This word, etc., up to: they also interpreted, he sent in.
9.32: 9.32 Arise. The same, question 46. And now arise by night, you and your people with you, and lie in ambush. Some Latin texts have you shall hasten, etc., up to: God on the fourth day made the sun.
10.1: 10.1 After Abimelech. Augustine, question 47 on Judges. How was the uncle of Abimelech a man of the tribe of Issachar, etc., up to: that the flesh of the Lord might be propagated not only from the royal but also from the priestly stock.
11.1: 11.1 Augustine, question 49 on Judges. Jephthah is interpreted opening, etc., up to: because they do not keep the precepts of the law and as it were do not show fidelity to the husband.
11.3: 11.3 He dwelt in the land of Tob. The same, ibid. In a good land, that is, or rather the best. For what in Greek is so, in Latin is called best. This is interpreted Tob, where the resurrection seems to be understood. For what land is better than the earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption? The same, ibid. Before the passion he ate with publicans and sinners, etc., up to: that they may be justified and learn his ways. In those days. The same, ibid. Those who had cast off Christ, etc., up to: that by old age the last times may be signified.
11.8: 11.8 And the princes said. Augustine, ibid. Something like this was prefigured in Joseph, etc., up to: in which his kingdom shall have no end. And fight. Augustine: That Jephthah is sought as leader against the children of Ammon, that when they are conquered those who desired to fight under him as leader may be freed: because Ammon is interpreted son of my people, or people of sorrow; either those enemies are signified who from that same nation remained in unbelief; or all those predestined to Gehenna: where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, as for a people of sorrow. Although the people of sorrow are fittingly understood to be the devil and his angels: either because they acquire eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves are assigned to eternal misery.
11.9: 11.9 I will be your. The same, ibid. That is, the king whom that nation did not yet have in the time of the judges, etc., up to: but Jephthah signified him who is the true king. The same: King, namely as was written in the title of the cross, etc., up to: as those who are contained in the volumes of Kings. Are not the things which he possesses, etc. Is not whatever Chemosh gave you to inherit?
11.29: 11.29 And going round Gilead. Augustine, question 49 on Judges. Gilead is interpreted casting away, etc., up to: which he signifies by saying both from the watchtower of Gilead passing over and passing over to the children of Ammon.
11.30: 11.30 If you deliver the children of Ammon. Augustine, ibid. Whomever Jephthah thought of, he does not seem to have thought of his daughter; for he would not say: Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me, etc. For he indicates that he was hindered from fulfilling what he had thought of. But whom could he have thought of who had no sons? Did he think of his wife, and God did not wish this to happen, and not to leave it unpunished; lest anyone afterward dare it: and so that by great providence from what happened a great sacrament of the Church might be figured. From both, then, the prophecy is adapted: both what the one vowing thought, and what befell him unwilling. For if he thought of his wife, the wife of Christ is the Church. But because this Jephthah's wife could not be a virgin, in that the daughter rather met him, the rashness of the vow did not remain unavenged, and the virginity of the Church was figured, to whom it is said: Daughter, your faith has made you safe, go in peace (Luke 7). Augustine, question 49. Concerning Jephthah's daughter there is usually a great question, etc., up to: so that all that was done afterward seems to be understood as works of the Spirit of the Lord who came upon him. The same: But among praiseworthy men, etc., up to: that it be not avoided altogether, but only deferred, he labors. Isidore, on Judges, vol. 5: Jephthah signifies Christ, because, departing from the face of his brothers, that is, the Jews, he received principality among the nations, because he fulfilled all the sacraments of human salvation as though sworn: and offered his own flesh as a daughter for the salvation of Israel. He swore, moreover, to the Father and vowed according to that: As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob, namely that he would fulfill the sacrament of religion in the passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race. These things were so done through Christ that they seem to have been completed for the religion of the oath.
11.37: 11.37 And I will bewail, etc. And he did to her, etc. Augustine: The chaste virgin, that is, the Church, etc., up to: on account of whom the two testaments are also spoken of. Thence the custom grew. Augustine, question 49. As to what was done by command in Israel, that from day to day they gathered to lament the daughter of Jephthah, four days in the year, I do not think it signifies something after the fulfilled holocaust, which will be in eternal life, but the past times of the Church, in which the mourning were blessed. By the four days is figured its universality: on account of the four parts of the world through which it is spread far and wide. As to the propriety of the history, I do not think the Israelites decreed this except because they understood that in it the judgment of God was shown rather to strike the father, lest anyone thereafter vow such a sacrifice. For why was lamentation decreed, if that vow is one of joy?
12.7: 12.7 And Jephthah judged, etc. Augustine: As those two months on account of the seventy days signify the number six of the six ages, so here sixfold seven, drawn out, figures the same, as far as the six ages of the world are concerned; for six times seven is forty-two, nor is it in vain that Jephthah himself judged the people six years.
13.2: 13.2 But you shall conceive, etc. Isidore, on Judges. Samson has certain things as a type of Christ, etc., up to: and it was said of Christ also through the prophet: The sun of justice shall rise upon you, and healing in his wings.
13.3: 13.3 Nor unclean. Augustine, question 50. Unclean is the dissolution of discipline which had begun in Israel, and had already weakened them to eat those things which God had forbidden in animals: for they were already passing even to the worship of idols. Augustine, question 52 on Judges. As to what the woman says was told her by the angel, etc., up to: the Nazirites observed on certain days, vowing and paying the vow.
13.19: 13.19 He took therefore. Augustine, question 53. As to what Scripture says, that Manoah did not know it was the angel of the Lord, etc., up to: that he be delivered to the enemies for forty years.
13.20: 13.20 Which. Gregory, Morals, book 5, ch. 23. What is it that at the vision of the angel the man is fearful, the woman bold, but that when heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit indeed shakes itself with dread, yet hope presumes. For hope rises to dare greater things from the very cause by which the spirit is troubled, which sees the things that are above first, because when the mind, so lifted up, beholds the higher things of heavenly secrets, all the solidity of human strength trembles. Augustine, question 54 on Judges. What is it that after the angel was manifested to Manoah and his wife, etc., up to: not to receive the sacrifice, but himself to be the sacrifice.
14.5: 14.5 Samson therefore went down, etc. Isidore, on Judges, vol. 5, ch. 8. Samson, when he went toward the foreigners to seek a wife, killed a lion: and Christ, about to call the Church from the nations, conquered the devil, who said: Rejoice, because I have overcome the world (John 16). From the mouth of the slain lion a honeycomb is drawn, because, as we see, the kings of the earthly kingdom, who before raged against Christ, their ferocity now destroyed, proclaim the sweetness of the Gospel and provide defenses.
15.8: 15.8 And he struck them, etc. Augustine, question 55 on Judges. Seventy: Samson struck the foreigners shin upon thigh, that is, so marvelously that, astonished, they placed the shin of one leg upon the thigh of the other.
15.12: 15.12 Swear. Augustine, question 56 on Judges. What is it that Samson says to the men of Judah, etc., up to: unless learned by hearing or reading, so also the manners of speech.
15.16: 15.16 With the jawbone. Gregory, Morals, book 13, ch. 6. The jawbone of the ass signifies the preachers. For our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of the preachers, slew the carnal from their vices, and the jawbone cast to the ground afterward poured forth waters: because the bodies of the preachers given over to death showed great miracles to the peoples.
16.1: 16.1 He went also, etc. Gregory, Homily 21 on the Gospels. Whom in this deed Samson, etc., up to: and ascending penetrated the kingdoms of heaven.
16.19: 16.19 And he called a barber. Isidore, on Judges, vol. 5, ch. 6. That the deceitful woman shaved Samson's head, etc., up to: and the contest prepared, to the end he will most strongly triumph over the demons. Gregory, Morals, book 27, ch. 13. Samson, his eyes lost, is assigned by the Philistines to the mill, etc., up to: they send outside into the round of labor.
16.30: 16.30 And many more. Gregory, Morals, book 29, ch. 7. In this place Christ is signified through Samson, etc., up to: by dying he laid low all together.
17.5: 17.5 And he made an ephod and teraphim, etc. Jerome, epistle 130, vol. 1. In the volume of Judges, etc., up to: is shown to have made through teraphim.
18.7: 18.7 They came to Laish, etc. Jerome, book on Hebrew places. Laish, the children of Dan, etc., up to: near Eshtaol.
19.25: 19.25 He brought out his concubine to them, etc. Augustine, City of God, ch. 34. A concubine is sometimes used for a wife. For Hagar and Keturah are called both wives and concubines of Abraham.
20.18: 20.18 They consulted. Gregory, Morals, book 24, ch. 13. He who does not judge himself, etc., up to: but be rigid against itself, yet submissive to all the good.
21.1: 21.1 The children of Israel also swore in Mizpah, etc.
